text: The landlord's note sat on the blotter, unopened since Tuesday; we had an understanding. The radiator had lost its fight with the cold and was lying there.
Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn't going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. I lit a cigarette off the lamp and let the smoke do the worrying.
The landlady's bill was folded under the telephone. I'd see it every time the thing didn't ring. I decided not to open it until it did.
I owed six weeks on the office, and the cold came in round the window sash to collect.
The rent envelope had a little window, so the amount could look out at me unopened. Rain ticked against the glass, steady, uninvited.
I had money in the desk drawer for once. I'd opened the drawer twice to make sure, and once more just to visit.
The whiskey in the bottom drawer was the good kind, bought and not borrowed. I poured one and didn't count what was left.
Flush enough to run the radiator all night, and the radiator, sensing money, actually worked. The cold stayed on its side of the glass.
New bills sat stiff in my coat pocket, smelling of the bank, my favorite smell. Moonlight came in flat across the blotter, and for once I didn't mind what it showed.
My head kept its own time, behind the clock over the safe and louder. I put the lamp low and thanked it.
The coffee I'd made was cold by the time I remembered it. I drank it anyway; it was lighter than holding my head.
Last night's cigarette sat half-smoked in the ashtray, and my stomach asked to be excused from the room. I cracked the window and let the rain-smell in instead.
The telephone stayed quiet, which was its own mercy; one ring would have finished me. Cold came up through the floorboards, and I let the headache have the room.
My knuckle had split open again in the same place as last month, which was at least consistent of it. Frost had crept across the window glass from the inside.
The mirror over the washbasin showed more of the night before than I wanted explained. I turned the lamp away from it.
I favored the side that still ached and lowered myself into the chair in three stages, like a drawbridge.
My jaw had gone from purple to a color nobody sells paint in. Even the low lamp showed that much. The mirror could wait for morning.
The last case's photographs were still in the drawer. I hadn't worked out whether to file them or burn them. Either felt like more trouble than the marriage was worth.
A woman's calling card sat under the paperweight, three days after I'd stopped needing it. I left it there instead of admitting I'd forgotten to throw it out.
The ledger lay open at a column of hotel names, each one some husband's idea of a secret. Fog had come up thick enough to blur the streetlamp across the way, and I let it blur the ledger too.
Two weeks of somebody else's marriage had left my coat smelling of hotel soap, and the fog hadn't shifted it. I hung it by the door to think about what it had done.
I hadn't slept since the night before the night before. The clock over the door had stopped pretending that mattered to it. I let it keep its own count.
I had no plans for bed and had stopped pretending otherwise. I kept the lamp burning for the company more than the light.
The tenants below had gone home, and the building's quiet had moved in and made itself comfortable. Through the window the sky had gone perfectly clear. I hadn't looked up in a while.
Sleep was a stranger I'd stopped waiting up for. The window showed my reflection and the dark behind it; the dark looked better rested.
I gave up on bed around eleven and made my peace with the desk chair, which had never once let me sleep. The stairs outside creaked twice, some tenant getting home.
The retainer was still folded in my breast pocket. I'd checked for it twice on the walk up, which wasn't like me. I put it in the drawer, where it would keep its shape better than I would.
Money sat in the office for once instead of a promise of it. I lit a cigarette slowly, like a man with a bank account. The cold stayed outside the glass where it belonged.
I'd paid the landlady on my way up, and she'd counted it on the landing in front of me. The stairs felt shorter for it. The office looked the same as always, which was its own kind of relief.
The fee sat on the blotter where I'd dropped it, more money than the desk usually saw in a month. I left the lamp burning longer than I needed, so the two of them could get acquainted.
The rent was two weeks late, and the landlady had stopped knocking about it, which was worse. Outside the window the night was clear, the street lamps sharp as far as the corner.
I counted my wallet twice, hoping for a mistake, and it came to eleven dollars both times. The rent was thirty. Fog stood against the window and hid the street, which suited me.
More money in the drawer than bills on the desk. The telephone company and the landlady were paid, and some was left over. I didn't know what people did with that.

I had bought a new ribbon for the typewriter and a carton of cigarettes, and there was still money in my pocket. Fog had come up off the river and blotted out the street. I lit one and did not count what was left in the carton.
The whiskey was a mistake I had made slowly, over most of the evening. When the window let in a hard, clear moon, I pulled the shade down on it.
My head ached from the night before. I'd sent two aspirin after it, and they hadn't found it yet. The fog outside made the street lamp a smudge, and my eyes were grateful.
Two fingers on my left hand had swollen since the afternoon, and I held them in a glass of water from the tap. The night outside was clear, and the moon showed every smear on the window.
My ribs hurt when I breathed deep, so I breathed shallow. Rain ran down the window in the lamplight, and I sat and listened to it and did not move much.
The husband had paid, the wife had cried, and I had the photographs to show for it. Out the window the sky was clear. I put the envelope of prints face down in the drawer.
I had spent three nights in a hotel corridor watching one door, and the cold was still in my feet. The radiator had quit again, like it was the one working. I kept my coat on.
I had tried the cot in the back room, and the cot had won. It was too cold to sleep and too late to go anywhere, so I sat at the desk with my coat on and the lamp low.
Sleep would not come, and I had stopped sending for it. Rain had been at the window all evening with a lot to say, and I let it talk.
The last client had paid in full, and I owed nobody. Feet on the desk, I enjoyed it carefully, like holding somebody else's baby. Outside, a clear, still night.

I had paid the landlady, the telephone company and the man who sold me coffee, and there was still money in the drawer. Fog had filled the street as high as the second-floor windows. It could stay there.
